UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                    )                      Docket No. ER26-3515-000



              COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST OF THE NRG COMPANIES



       Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedures,1 the NRG Companies2 (“NRG”) respectfully submit these

comments and limited protest in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) August 13,

2026, filing proposing to establish interim resource adequacy service (“IRAS”) and a large load

registry to address system reliability (“PJM IRAS Filing” or “IRAS Filing”).

       In general, NRG supports PJM’s efforts to provide certainty and clarity to market

participants and New Large Loads3 that do not bring new supply into the PJM market. NRG also

supports PJM’s efforts to articulate rules pertaining to the curtailment of New Large Loads that

       However, PJM’s proposal contains elements that are unjust, unreasonable, unduly

discriminatory, and must be revised. These consist of (i) PJM’s permanent exclusion of every

Demand Resource4 that has ever supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery Year

and (ii) the requirement for new capacity serving New Large Loads to bid into the capacity

market as a price-taker for 10 years without certain necessary protections for asset owners.

Finally, there are a number of clarifications NRG seeks related to the IRAS requirements around

Demand Resources.



I.     ABOUT NRG

       Through various subsidiaries, NRG owns or controls over 9 GW of generation in PJM as

well as generation in adjacent markets that can be imported into the PJM market. Additionally,

NRG subsidiaries provide retail power throughout PJM and two NRG subsidiaries provide

Demand Resources in PJM. Thus, NRG actively participates in the organized markets

administered by PJM, including the PJM capacity market.



II.    BACKGROUND

       The PJM IRAS Filing creates a new supplemental capacity product through which New

Large Loads may provide a load reduction service during periods of insufficient capacity instead

(“DER”) Capacity Aggregation Resources, as the terms are defined by the PJM OATT, as
“Demand Resources” to improve readability, but is not intended to refer only to Demand

                                                2
 of participating in the Base Residual Auction (“BRA”). IRAS resources will be issued

curtailment instructions prior to PJM calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management. For

providing the reduction, PJM proposes an IRAS rate equal to 50% of the Non-Performance

Charge Rate, with flexibility for Electric Distributors and states to reduce the rate or for eligible

New Large Loads to waive compensation entirely.

       Instead of participating as an IRAS resource, New Large Loads may instead meet their

capacity obligations through a Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) option. BYONC is

defined as megawatts of new Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”) that meet the eligibility criteria set

forth in Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI.5 A single physical resource may support multiple

BYONC arrangements with different New Large Loads, and a New Large Load may enter into

BYONC arrangements with discrete resources.6 BYONC must be supported by: (1) a new-build

generation resource (including resources obtaining Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred

from deactivated resources); (2) incremental capacity from an uprate; (3) incremental capacity

from Surplus Interconnection Service; (4) repowering of a deactivated resource that deactivated

prior to April 10, 2026; or (5) incremental capacity from a fuel-type change.7 BYONC may also

be supported by Planned Demand Resources or Planned DER Capacity Aggregation

Resources. However, PJM has proposed to only permit BYONC to be supported by Demand

Resources if those resources “did not previously support a capacity commitment or reduce the

amount of capacity needed to meet the PJM Reliability Requirement … for or prior to the

supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery Year.

       Each BYONC must participate as a price taker ($0/MW offer) in BRAs for 10

consecutive Delivery Years, starting with the first Delivery Year of the arrangement. BYONC is

also subject to the capacity must-offer requirement and is prohibited from seeking an exception

to provide an external sale during the 10-year period. BYONC supported by a Demand Resource

or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource also has a 10-year commitment, but the seller may

replace its BYONC obligation with a different qualifying resource, subject to conditions. This

provides a “bridge to power” allowing near-term demand-supported capacity to be eventually

replaced with new generation. Additionally, beginning with the 2029/30 Delivery Year, PJM

proposes to exclude from the VRR Curve the MW of New Large Loads that have not entered

into BYONC arrangements and do not have allocated capacity (IRAS resources), above and

beyond the MW included in the 2028/29 Delivery Year load forecast.

       BYONC BRA participation requirements (including the price-taker obligation) are

extinguished if IRAS is not needed for three consecutive Delivery Years. At that point, BYONC

resources become regular Capacity Resources, though still subject to the general capacity must-

offer requirement. If the PJM Region meets its reliability requirements for three consecutive

Delivery Years and then re-enters shortage, the “new” benchmark resets. Demand-side capacity

would then be measured against registration “in the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery

Year” in which PJM is again short of capacity.

 III.   COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE PJM IRAS FILING

       In general, NRG supports PJM’s IRAS Filing. PJM proposes to require Load Serving

Entities (“LSEs”) to “bring new capacity in an amount that equals or exceeds its New Large

Loads’ peak load or be subject to load reduction requests during Emergencies prior to Pre-

Emergency Load Management Response.”9 PJM notes that it is “currently short of capacity and

looking to reestablish healthy capacity reserve margin.”10 PJM’s approach is commonsense: New

Large Loads must be supported by Capacity Resources. Furthermore, NRG supports the

requirement that the BYONC capacity be “new” generation.

       NRG also supports PJM’s proposal to curtail New Large Loads before existing

customers, including Pre-Emergency and Emergency Demand Response customers. Specifically,

the PJM IRAS Filing provides that “PJM can call on IRAS load reductions prior to calling on

Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions Actions when needed to avoid a capacity

shortage.”11 As PJM notes, this provision does not identify the specific load that an Electric

Distributor must reduce.12 Rather, the Electric Distributor, in coordination with the appropriate

states and/or Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities, LSEs, and LSE customers, will

determine which loads should ultimately be curtailed.13 The proposed curtailment obligation

IV.    LIMITED PROTEST

       Pursuant to the Commission’s Rule 211,14 NRG provides the following limited protest.

As written, the tariff proposed by PJM fails to be just and reasonable and is unduly

discriminatory because it (i) excludes otherwise capable Demand Resources based on an

unwarranted permanent bar to such resources that have participated in any prior BRA; and

(ii) imposes an overly broad and unjust and unreasonable ten-year price-taker obligation on all

BYONC resources.

       PJM has consented to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify or sever any

element of the filing to the extent necessary, so long as the modification is consistent with PJM’s

overarching objectives.15 Thus, the Commission has authority to modify PJM’s proposed tariff in

the manner proposed by NRG by directing a compliance filing.16 NRG’s modest proposals do not

    A. New Demand Resources Should Be Permitted to Bid into the Market to Support
       New Large Loads Regardless of Prior Market Participation

        PJM states that new capacity, BYONC, is at a basic level, “megawatts of Unforced

Capacity” and thus is “consistent with how Capacity Resources under PJM’s capacity market

design are also MW and not the underlying physical resource.”18 PJM explains that BYONC is

“designed to offset the capacity need presented by the New Large Load.”19 PJM further explains

that “new capacity may be supported by generation, storage, or demand-side resources that meet

certain gating criteria.”20

        However, PJM’s “gating criteria” for BYONC applicable to Demand Resources include a

requirement that Planned Demand Resources “did not previously support a capacity commitment

or reduce the amount of capacity needed to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement … for

or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.”21 This means that PJM has permanently excluded

every Demand Resource that has ever supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery

       Under PJM’s proposal, a customer location that participated as a Demand Resource as far

back as 200624 and later ceased participation would be ineligible to participate as a BYONC

capacity resource. The ban on eligibility applies even if the ownership or occupancy at the

customer location has changed or if there are new flexibility capabilities. For example, a

customer location that ceased participation as a Demand Resource in 2010 and was no longer in

any way considered an existing capacity resource would be banned from participation in

BYONC. This exclusion is patently unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.25

storage resources that exited the market but could reactivate their Capacity Interconnection

       Taken together, these factors contradict how PJM proposes treating these resources.

Indeed, the flexible and voluntary nature of Demand Resource participation in the PJM capacity

       The IRAS Filing contemplates that, if the PJM Region meets its reliability requirements

for three consecutive Delivery Years and then re-enters shortage, the “new” benchmark resets. At

that point, the demand-side gating criterion measures against registration “in the Delivery Year

prior to the first Delivery Year” in which the PJM Region is short of capacity.38 Here, PJM itself

recognizes a lookback-window approach is workable and reasonable. There is no principled

justification for the asymmetry of applying a lookback in one context but not in the related

Demand Resources context. To address this unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory

treatment, NRG requests that the Commission adopt a three-year lookback window rather than a

permanent exclusion.39 Namely, PJM should permit Demand Resources that have not

participated in the three most recent BRAs to qualify for BYONC.

       The overly broad ineligibility is inconsistent with the policy announced by the Secretary

of Energy to leverage available backup generation to address the United States’ reliability

challenges and other grid challenges.40 There are gigawatts of backup generation that were once

eligible and did participate in demand response but subsequently discontinued participation.

       In short, a Demand Resource that chooses to re-enter the market still provides new

   B. Capacity Serving New Large Loads Should Not Be Required to Bid into the BRA as
      a Price Taker for 10 Years Without a Replacement Mechanism

       PJM proposes that “BYONC must participate, as a price taker (i.e. $0/MW offer) in RPM

Auctions for 10 consecutive Delivery Years.”42 PJM states that the BYONC arrangement “serves

as the commitment to provide [] capacity.”43 PJM further states that because the “resource is

already obligated to provide the capacity, its incremental, going-forward avoidable costs to

secure the RPM commitment are zero.”44 The ten-year price-taker obligation is not just and

reasonable as applied to all Capacity Resources, including generation, storage, and demand-side

resources. NRG’s protest on this point is not limited to Demand Resources. NRG requests that

market conditions evolve. As a result, this market construct is effectively designed to keep

       The Commission should direct PJM to include the opportunity for such costs to be

reflected in subsequent capacity auctions should conditions such as those described above arise.

The PJM Tariff already has mechanisms for other resources to reflect their costs through unit

specific Avoidable Cost Rate (“ACR”) offers.48 NRG proposes a similar approach here. This

would ensure in the limited cases where otherwise unforeseen circumstances are unaddressed or

are at issue in bilateral transactions, the resource owner has an opportunity (but not the

guarantee) to recover such unforeseen costs.49 The ACR approach also offers benefits to PJM

customers: (1) the market receives the benefit of the zero-offer price for ten years in most cases,

absent detailed showings; (2) in extraordinary circumstances, the Capacity Resource serving a

New Large Load is able to continue doing so while recovering exceptional and unforeseen costs;

(3) more economic resources are able to enter the market and replace highly inefficient Capacity

Resources; and (4) reliability is improved over the course of the IRAS-imposed commitments.50

V.     NRG SEEKS CLARIFICATION, OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE, TARIFF
       MODIFICATIONS, PERMITTING EXPANDED DEMAND RESPONSE
       CAPACITY TO BE TREATED AS NEW CAPACITY

       NRG has identified four areas in the IRAS Filing that lack clarity, and to the extent these

areas are inconsistent with NRG’s requested clarification, are unjust and unreasonable because

they are discriminatory. First, existing Demand Resources should be permitted to offer BYONC

in excess of prior capacity offers as “new” capacity. Second, any resource that would qualify as

“new” capacity can also be eligible to serve as replacement capacity for Demand Resources.

Third, curtailment-based Demand Resources should be eligible for BYONC without requiring

generation or storage assets at the location. Fourth, the methodology used to determine eligibility

of Demand Resources must be defined.

        In PJM, the quantum of Demand Resources that a customer can provide is capped at its

Peak Load Contribution (“PLC”).62 Individual contributions to an aggregator’s portfolio change

annually and may be difficult to predict more than one year into the future. Individual customer

volumes of participating demand response expands and contracts based upon PLC as well as

customer usage patterns. Businesses and homes change owners/tenants and new occupants may

decide to start or stop participation in demand response. Technology evolves. Equipment gets old

and may be replaced. Batteries, distributed generation, electric vehicles, etc., all can change

customer PLC and load reduction capabilities. This diversity and the ebb and flow of customer

demand response capabilities is managed by aggregators – who can add new customers to

replace customers who depart or whose flexible capability declines. However, in the aggregate,

the volume of the Demand Resource is reliable.
